text:
Summary
In Summary, Xenium data utilizes a gene panel of probes to assay the spatially-resolved expression of specific genes at a cellular or subcellular resolution within tissue samples. Samples used to generate Xenium data are either fresh frozen (FF) or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue samples. After sample preparation, imaging cycles are performed using a Xenium Analyzer. Cellular segmentation is performed to approximate boundaries between cells.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Assessing Quality, Normalization, and Expression Patterns in Spatially-Informed Gene Expression Data
text:
Data context

The data used in this case study are from Kwon et al. (2026) which collected dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) samples postmortem from neurotypical donors and donors with diagnosed schizophrenia. Samples were fresh frozen following collection prior to spatial transcriptomics dataset generation. Kwon et al. (2026) generated data using both the Visium and Xenium platforms, using analysis of the Visium data to inform what Xenium data to collect. Visium data was generated for all donors as explained in Supplementary Table 1 while Xenium data was generated for a subset of these donors. For donors where both Visium and Xenium datasets were generated, the tissue samples originated from the same fresh frozen tissue block or source for each donor, but the samples themselves (used to generate the data for each platform) are from adjacent tissue sections of each block. Since each platform requires its own slide mounting and chemical reagents, typically serial tissue sectioning is used to yield adjacent / comparable tissue samples that can be used for multiple experiments with different technologies.
Postmortem tissue samples from 24 donors were used to generate Xenium data. Twelve of those donors had been diagnosed with schizophrenia (denoted by SCZ within the study and this case study) while the other 12 were neurotypical (denoted by NTC within the study and CTRL within this case study).

This case study will work solely with the Xenium data, using only 6 of the 24 samples (3 CTRL and 3 SCZ).

We will work with a reduced number of samples in order to keep the size of the data more manageable. It’s important, especially in studies involving visualization of tissue sections, to work with multiple tissue sections per case (e.g., CTRL vs SCZ) to make sure that signal is not an artifact of how that sample was processed or cut and instead is generalizable across tissue sections/samples.


Matching sample demographics

Typically studies match donor demographics between case cohorts (e.g., having comparable average ages or number of individuals of each sex). Kwon et al. (2026) does this for all of the samples overall as well as the subset of samples that were processed with the Xenium platform, reporting the information in Supplementary Table 1.


The Xenium spatial transcriptomics data represents cellular mRNA counts for panel-targeted genes, mapping the transcripts from those genes to the cellular spatial locations in the tissue (where the probes bound, signifying expression). As such there are 3 main data types or files that we will be working with.

Tissue/sample metadata
Spatial coordinates of cells in the sample
mRNA counts of panel-targeted transcripts for each cell




The panel genes

The panel targets 300 genes using probes designed specifically to target transcripts of these genes:

Six genes (A2M, MAPK3, PLP1, RCAN2, SERPINA3, SOX2-OT) overlap multiple categories within the panel, leading to a total of 300 unique genes represented in the panel. An additional 68 genes already in the panel were also marked as cell type marker genes (beyond the original 35) following further literature review. This can be explored in Supplementary Table 8.

Specific Data Files

Specific data files that we will work with in this case study include files for each of the aspects of the Xenium data:

Sample metadata
Spatial coordinates
mRNA counts


We will be fetching the Xenium generated data (spatial coordinates and mRNA counts) from GEO in the Data Import section of the case study. The project’s GEO accession number for the Xenium data is GSE307404. Each sample has its own specific GEO accession number which we will use to fetch the data rather than fetching data for all 24 samples.

The -cells.parquet and -cell_feature_matrix.h5 files are the important files going forward.


Sample metadata
The sample metadata file that we will be working with combines the metadata from Supplementary Table 1 with the GEO accession number for each sample. When using secondary data, it is common for sample metadata to be available in supplementary information. You may need to combine multiple tables of information.


Expansion of metadata from Supplementary Table 1

We previously created a file for the Xenium samples which maps each sample’s GEO Accession Number to the Brain Number ID (geo_to_spatial_samples.csv) and united this with the data from Supplementary Table 1 because we will need the GEO accession number in order to fetch the spatial coordaintes and mRNA counts for each sample. However, the sample metadata file provided in the supplementary table only includes the Brain Number ID (Br####).
The files for this project follow the naming pattern of {sample specific GEO accession number}_{sample Brain Number ID}-{file type specific pattern},

Listed files from GEO accession number GSE307404 (all Xenium data from this project) with list.files() function for one of the file types.
Used stringr::str_replace() function to the specific pattern for that file type with an empty string (""), removing all but the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID (separated by an underscore) for each sample.
Used strsplit("_") function to separate the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID for each string.
Used do.call(rbind.data.frame, .) to create a data frame with the sample GEO accession numbers in the first column and their associated Brain Number IDs in the second column.
Set the column names.
Saved to a .csv file.

Alternatively, we could create this map using the title and geo_accession columns from the pData(gse[[1]]) output we saw earlier.

The combined data from Supplementary Table 1 and the GEO to Brain Number ID map is contained in the file spatial_samples.csv. The spatial_samples.csv file is a file with a header (column names) where values are separated by a comma (.csv). The contents of each column are explained in the following table:



Variable
Details




BrainNumberID
An identifier representing which donor brain the sample originates from. Follows the pattern “Br####”


Race
Demographic information about donors. All samples are “CAUC” for caucasian.


Sex
Demographic information about donors. “M” for male or “F” for female.


Age
Demographic information about donors. Number / decimal representing age of donor in years.


RIN
RNA Integrity Number. Number / decimal representing the quality of the fresh frozen block tissue samples. Generally, Visium and Xenium recommend brain tissues have an observed RIN of 4+ (though older resources may recommend 7+) (Grases and Porta-Pardo (2026)). Lower RINs may lead to reduced sensitivity.


PMI
Postemortem Interval. Number / decimal representing the time interval between the donor’s death and the sample extraction and freezing from that donor. Typically reported in hours, but could be reported in days or another measurement of time. To promote greater fresh frozen block tissue quality, generally it is recommended to minimize the post mortem interval


PrimaryDx
Demographic information about donors representing the primary diagnosis. “Control” for neurotypical donors and “Schizophrenia” for donors diagnosed with schizophrenia.


Visium
“YES” or “NO” for whether Visium data was generated for this sample. All samples are “YES”.


Xenium
“YES” or “NO” for whether Xenium data was generated for this sample.


GEO
The GEO accession number for samples with Xenium data. NA for samples with only Visium data.



The demographic information is useful for data exploration. We will primarily be using the BrainNumberID, PrimaryDx, Xenium, and GEO variables.

The Xenium and GEO variables will be used to select a subset of samples of fetch the data for those samples from GEO.
The BrainNumberID and PrimaryDx variables will be used to create informative sample IDs so that we can more easily observe the case (e.g., CTRL or SCZ) of samples throughout our analysis.



Spatial coordinates
Classically, -cells.parquet files are used to store the spatial coordinates of the cells, specifically the {{ < glossary Centroid display=centroid > }} locations (or centers of the cells).
The .parquet file type is a departure from the normal way we would expect data to be stored. Often our file types (e.g., .csv) store data row by row with each row containing a complete record or set of related information about a specific sample, timepoint, etc. Instead, .parquet files store data column-by-column. This leads to more efficient storage and querying of large data files.
Additional information provided in this file is described by 10X genomics.


If -cells.parquet files are not available

Sometimes when you are using publicly available data rather than generating new datasets yourself, files that you may expect are not deposited or archived.
If .parquet files are not available, first check if cells.csv.gz is available as this is an alternate format of the typical file. If not, you can use a different Xenium output to calculate the centroids typically stored in the cells.parquet files. This will be explored further within a click to expand section in the Data Import section of the case study, but this alternate file type is also introduced here:
-cell_boundaries.csv.gz also stores spatial coordinates. Specifically these files have many rows per cell describing each vertex that is part of a polygon, where the polygon edges represent the borders of the cell. We can find the centroid of each cell by considering all of these polygon coordinates together. The contents of this file are the result of the nucleus segmentation algorithm that expands the nuclei DAPI-stained boundaries to determine cell boundaries.







Variable
Details




cell_id
A cell ID corresponding to the barcode variable in the mRNA counts data. Multiple rows will have the same cell_id value in these files.


vertex_x
The x-coordinate of a vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell.


vertex_y
The corresponding y-coordinate of that vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell.












Another file output that Xenium provides is nucleus_boundaries. This file is not sufficient for cell spatial coordinates because it’s only providing the boundaries of the nucleus rather than the cells. Nuclear positioning varies across cells, so you can’t make an assumption about the center of cell if you have coordinates for the nucleus.
These file types are described in greater detail by 10X genomics.


This case study will use the arrow package to work with -cells.parquet files for the spatial coordinates data.



mRNA counts
The data for the mRNA counts that we’ll be using is stored in -cell_feature_matrix.h5 files. This file type efficiently stores large amounts of data that are typically represented by large matrices (n rows for genes * m columns for cells with counts for a given gene in a specific cell stored at each intersection). Instead, .h5 files use nested named lists to store the data. Of important note, only non-zero counts are stored as well as the indices where those counts would be located in a matrix (e.g., indices for which genes and cell IDs they would correspond with). These nested named lists can be used to reconstruct the matrix structure of the data.
Note that “features” is an alternative word for genes in this field and will be used interchangeably throughout this case study.
We can use either the rhdf5::h5dump() function or the rhdf5::h5ls() function to get a look at the nested lists (and their names) for this data.

$matrix is the top list name

$barcodes – nested list under matrix; the cell IDs
$data – nested list under matrix; the non-zero counts
$features – nested list under matrix; has its own nested subparts relating to the rows/genes

$_all_tag_keys – “genome” for our data
$feature_type – specifies “Gene Expression” for the panel genes or Xenium QC probes/codewords such as negative control probe, negative control codeword, or unassigned codeword

$id – gene ID or control/probe ID for elements of $data
$name – gene name or control/probe name for elements of $data

$indices – nested list under matrix; zero-based row index for non-zero values found in $data (i equivalent for Matrix::sparseMatrix() function used in the Data Import section of the case study)
$indptr – nested list under matrix; zero-based index for $data and $indices where columns start (p equivalent of Matrix::sparseMatrix() function in the Data Import section of the case study)
$shape – nested list under matrix; dimensions of the data (number of genes or features X number of cells).

Note that the number of cells >>>>> number of genes (Xenium panel with limited number of genes)
Note that the product of the dimensions will be greater than the length of $data since this data format is representing non-zero counts only and therefore is a sparse representation



The most important parts of this file for us will be barcodes, data, features$name, indices, indptr, and shape. Each of these will be used as we build sparse matrices from the .h5 formatted data.
For more information about the .h5 file format, consider this 10X Genomics resource.


If -cells_feature_matrix.h5 files are not available

Alternative formats for mRNA counts that may be provided as Xenium outputs (MEX or Zarr) are discussed here with specific explanations for Zarr files here. Tools such as Rarr, zarr, XeniumIO, or Seurat may be useful for working with these file types.


This case study will use the rhdf5 and Matrix packages to work with cell_feature_matrix.h5 files for the mRNA counts data



General note on variety of Xenium outputs
Xenium produces a variety of output files. Not all of these will be shared / deposited into an archive. While some file types may be more usual or preferred by some in the field (e.g., because it’s more efficient to store or it’s a file type they are more comfortable with), there doesn’t appear to be a specific industry standard or accepted practice on files to always use. For example, morphology images (likely stained with DAPI to mark nuclei) are often output but are not always shared. An output may be shared as a .csv file instead of a .parquet file or as a Zarr file instead of an .h5 file. It may seem like you can’t proceed if you don’t see the file types you expect, but it’s not necessarily a lost cause. Make sure that you understand:

What files are available and what they represent about the data. You may be able to use an alternate file type for a specific aspect of the data (e.g., spatial coordiantes).
What file types your downstream tools expect or can work with.
If you can use a file type that you have in place of a file type that you or a downstream tool usually expects, or at least wrangle it to meet your needs.
What (if any) specialized packages are necessary to read in and work with certain file types.



Reproducibility Considerations


If you need a specific file but don’t see it in an archive, contact the study personnel and ask if that file can be added. Data reuse benefits the scientific community and promotes reproducible, robust, and generalizable scientific discovery.

What spatialGE is looking for

spatialGE provides the user flexibility in how they import their data. Users can either provide file paths or they can provide named lists with each list containing data frames for each sample. To better understand the data we have and are working with, we will provide named lists of data frames for both the spatial coordinates and the mRNA/feature counts.

Spatial coordinates
For spatial coordinates, each data frame should have:

3 columns

Cell IDs
X coordinate for the center of the cell
Y coordiante for the center of the cell

One row per each unique cell ID; let’s say we have m cells



mRNA counts
For the mRNA counts, each data frame should have:

n rows

1 for each feature
let’s say we have n features.

(m+1) columns

1 for each cell
For our spatial coordinates, we said we had m cells
Add 1 because the first column will list the feature/gene names











Both of these will be stored in separate named lists where the names correspond to samples, and each sample has its own data frame.


Sample metadata
spatialGE also requires sample information. We will provide sample names / metadata where the sample names match those used in the named lists. The sample names will be in the first column of the samples metadata data frame.

Spatial Coordinates

decompress_read_parquet <- function(samples_metadata, sample){
  #Build file paths
  gz_file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                         "-cells.parquet.gz"))
  
  decompressed_file <- str_replace(gz_file, ".gz", "")

  #Decompress
  R.utils::gunzip(gz_file, destname = decompressed_file, remove = FALSE, skip = TRUE)

  #Read in
  df <- arrow::read_parquet(decompressed_file)

  #Remove the decompressed file because we no longer need it
  file.remove(decompressed_file)
  
  #Select columns of interest
  centroids <- df %>%
    select(cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid)

  #reclaim some R resources
  rm(df, gz_file, decompressed_file)
  gc()

  #Return
  return(centroids)

}

spatial_coords <- lapply(1:nrow(samples_metadata), function(x) decompress_read_parquet(samples_metadata, samples_metadata$sampleID[x]))

(with st_as_sf()) we convert the data frame into a simple feature object so that we can work within a spatial context (to compute the cell’s centroid) for non-spatial data structures

We grab x and y coordinates for the centroids, storing them in their own columns
We store the Cell IDs and centroid coordinates as a dataframe for that sample

Note, will show in a click to expand section that rhdf5::h5dump can be used to look at the headers of the data, especially because we have to provide a “name” in the reading function and knowing that name requires knowing the headers

We create a function to use for all 6 of the samples …. for each sample ….
We read in the corresponding cell feature matrix file
We build a sparse matrix, using the elements of the h5 file that correspond to each argument (as explained in the data description section above)
We expand it to be a dense matrix that can be turned into a dataframe
We set the row names to be the feature names from the h5 file
We set the column names to be the cell IDs from the h5 file
We also move the rownames to the first column and name it “genes” because spatialGE looks for gene names in the first column, not as rownames, making sure they are unique..
Finally we store this matrix in our named list for that sample



Turn this into an lapply statement instead of a for loop, utilizing a function for the main steps.

read_rna <- function(samples_metadata, sample){

  h5file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                        "-cell_feature_matrix.h5"))
                              

  rna_h5data <- rhdf5::h5read(h5file, name = "matrix")

  rna_mat <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = rna_h5data$indices,
                       p = rna_h5data$indptr,
                       x = as.integer(rna_h5data$data),
                       dims = rna_h5data$shape,
                       index1 = FALSE) %>%
      as.matrix() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      `rownames<-`(rna_h5data$features$name) %>%
      `colnames<-`(rna_h5data$barcodes) %>%
      rownames_to_column("genes")

  rm(rna_h5data, h5file)
  gc()

  return(rna_mat)
}

rnacounts_input <- lapply(1:nrow(samples_metadata), function(x) read_rna(samples_metadata, samples_metadata$sampleID[x]))
names(rnacounts_input) <- samples_metadata$DxID

The STlist object is an S4 class in R. This means that the object has “slots”. Slots are accessed using an @, rather than a $.

text:
Filtering

Using Control Probes and Codewords
First we create a function that we can use with lapply that takes the filtering thresholds that we found previously as well as the counts matrix as inputs. Notice that the thresholds are named arguments meaning they have default values set to the exact variables we were working with earlier. We find the combined expression within each cell of each of the three associated controls using column sums and identify the cell IDs where the combined expression of any one of these types of controls is greater than or equal to the 99th percentile threshold. Finally, we take a union of the identified cell IDs.
By calling this function with lapply, we’ll have named list (to_remove_all) where the sample name stores a vector of cell IDs that should be removed for that sample.
We use a for loop to then loop through the sample names and actually filter the cell IDs within the count matrix. Recall that the cells correspond to the columns in the count matrix. Our filter is specifically using an exclamation point (!) to specify that if a column name is not the list of cell IDs to be filtered, then keep it.

findOverlap <- function(mat, negcp = negcontrol_probe_cutoff, negcc = negcontrol_cdwd_cutoff, ucc = unassigned_cdwd_cutoff){
    which_negcp <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlProbe"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcp))
    which_negcc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlCodeword"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcc))
    which_ucc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "Unassigned"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= ucc))

    to_remove <- union(union(which_negcp, which_negcc), which_ucc)

    return(to_remove)
}

to_remove_all <- lapply(scz_spatial@counts, function(x) findOverlap(x))

for (sample_name in names(to_remove_all)){
    scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]][,!colnames(scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]]) %in% to_remove_all[[sample_name]]]
}

Color Palettes
I tested several color palettes and settled on PuBuGn for several reasons. (Note: this could be a cool side quest to include in the case study)

Easier to distinguish changes in expression (e.g., up vs down regulated). BuRd and Spectral were best for this otherwise.

combine_counts_annot <- function(matannot, matcount, sample_name, gene_name){
    full_join(
        matannot[[sample_name]][,c("libname", "annot")],
        matcount[[sample_name]][gene_name, ] %>% 
            data.frame() %>% 
            rownames_to_column("libname")
    ) %>% `colnames<-`(c("libname", "annot", sample_name))
}

use_combined_data <- function(mat, gene_name, use = "violin", samples = c("Br1139SCZ", "Br5314CTRL")){
  combined_data <- bind_rows(combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[1], gene_name),
                             combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[2], gene_name)) %>%
                      pivot_longer(starts_with("Br"),
                                   values_to = "tr_counts",
                                   names_to = "sample") %>%
                      drop_na()

  if (use == "violin"){
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = sample, 
               y = tr_counts, 
               fill = sample)) + 
        geom_violin() + 
        facet_wrap(~annot, scales = "free_y") + 
        theme_bw() + 
        scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.6) + 
        ggtitle(gene_name) +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    )
  } else if (use == "summary"){
    table_length <- length(unique(combined_data$annot)) * 2
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        group_by(annot, sample) %>% 
        summarize(
              min_exp = min(tr_counts), 
              max_exp = max(tr_counts), 
              avg_exp = mean(tr_counts),
              median_exp = median(tr_counts),
              var_exp = var(tr_counts)
        ) %>% 
    print(n=table_length)
    )
  } else {
    message("No other downstream uses supported besides 'violin' and 'summary'")
  }
}
